    How this works
    

      
Without a seed, every number comes from crypto.getRandomValues. To land in a range of
        size n the page takes a 32-bit draw — or a 53-bit one for ranges past four billion — and
        discards it if it falls in the short leftover stretch beyond the last whole multiple of
        n, so every number in the range has exactly the same chance. Ranges run to about nine
        quadrillion either side of zero, the largest whole numbers JavaScript holds exactly.

      
No repeats draws without putting anything back: the page runs a partial
        Fisher–Yates shuffle over the range without ever writing the whole range out, so ten numbers from
        a billion cost the same as ten from a hundred. Asking for more numbers than the range holds is
        refused, since there are not that many to give. Sort orders the result after the
        draw; it never changes which numbers came out.

      
A seed makes the draw repeatable: the same seed with the same settings gives the
        same numbers on any device, which is how a raffle or a sample can be checked afterwards by someone
        who was not there. The seed is hashed into a small generator, sfc32, which is statistically sound but
        not secret — anyone who knows the seed knows the numbers, so publish the seed after the draw, not
        before, and never use a seeded draw for a password or a key. Without a seed, nothing can reproduce
        a draw, not even this page.

      
Draws are capped at 10,000 numbers at a time. Nothing is sent and nothing is stored; the Dark
        and language buttons keep their own settings in this browser's local storage.
